title: CFA Ethics 41: Standard I(D) - when conduct outside work touches professional standing
subtitle: The line between private life and the profession, and three signs that make a private matter a professional one
whyItMatters: This is the only standard reaching conduct outside the scope of work, so it is also where misunderstanding runs in both directions: either assuming private life is entirely out of scope, or assuming every personal failing is caught.
openingQuestion: Which conduct outside work does Standard I(D) apply to?
openingOptions: All personal conduct, because CFA members must set an example
Conduct bearing on honesty and professional competence
None, because private life sits outside the standards
Only conduct already convicted by a court in a final judgment
explanation: Standard I(D) is not a code of personal morality in general. It draws a circle around three things bearing directly on whether you deserve to be trusted with other people's money: honesty, trustworthiness, and professional competence. Cheating in a university exam, falsifying an application, or defrauding someone in a private transaction all fall within scope - not because they are bad in general but because they say something about how this person behaves when there is an opportunity and nobody is watching. An ordinary civil dispute or a traffic incident, by contrast, does not.

summary.keyIdea: Three criteria - honesty, trustworthiness, professional competence - apply to conduct outside work as well, whenever that conduct says something about those three qualities.
summary.commonMistake: Assuming private matters are irrelevant. Personal tax fraud goes straight to the honesty criterion, even though it happens outside working hours.

application.title: The boundary
application.message: Not every personal failing falls in scope. The question is whether the conduct says anything about others' ability to entrust money to you.

sections.text: Standard I(D) extends professional ethics beyond working hours - but not as far as many people assume, and knowing its boundary matters as much as knowing its content.
Three criteria that define the scope

Conduct outside work falls in scope only where it says something about those three. Cheating in a university exam, falsifying an application, defrauding someone in a private transaction all qualify - not because they are bad in general, but because they show how this person behaves when there is an opportunity and nobody is watching.

sections.label: Outside the scope
sections.text: An ordinary civil dispute, a traffic incident, or personal lifestyle choices unrelated to those three criteria. Standard I(D) is not a general code of personal morality.

Two points are often misunderstood. First, no criminal conviction is needed for a violation - evidence of the conduct is enough. Second, the logic underneath the standard is that behaviour in one context predicts behaviour in another, so the final question always reduces to one thing: should other people's money be entrusted to this person.

sections.title: The same kind of private matter, differing in what it says
sections.subtitle: The criterion is honesty, trustworthiness and professional competence - not how serious it sounds

concepts.vi: Khai man bằng cấp trong hồ sơ xin việc ở một ngành khác
concepts.en: Falsifying qualifications on a job application in another industry: in scope
concepts.def: Nothing to do with investment work, but it speaks directly to honesty. It falls under Standard I(D) wherever it happened.

concepts.vi: Một tranh chấp hợp đồng dân sự với hàng xóm
concepts.en: A civil contract dispute with a neighbour: out of scope
concepts.def: It may be noisy and prolonged, but it says nothing about honesty or professional competence. Standard I(D) is not a general reputation clause.

concepts.vi: Vỡ nợ cá nhân do rủi ro kinh doanh
concepts.en: Personal insolvency from business risk: usually out of scope
concepts.def: A business failure is not dishonesty. But where it comes with concealing assets or misstating things to creditors, that concealment is the violation.

concepts.vi: Gian lận trong một kỳ thi bất kỳ
concepts.en: Cheating in any examination: in scope
concepts.def: It touches both honesty and competence - and if it is the CFA exam, it breaches Standard VII(A) at the same time.

sections.label: No conviction required
sections.text: Standard I(D) does not wait for the justice system. Evidence of the conduct is enough to constitute a violation, because the duty here is to the profession rather than to the state. That also means the reverse holds: an acquittal in a criminal case does not automatically clear the matter, if the evidence of the conduct remains.

Because what the client is buying is that person.

realWorldExample.company: Why alcohol or substance misuse can fall in scope
realWorldExample.description: On its own it does not. It falls under Standard I(D) when it affects professional competence - making investment decisions while impaired, or letting the condition compromise duties to clients. This is the clearest illustration of the standard's general principle: it does not judge a lifestyle, it asks whether the conduct leaves you unable to perform your professional duties.

quiz.question: Which three criteria does Standard I(D) draw its circle around?
options: Honesty, obeying the law, and community contribution
Honesty, trustworthiness, and professional competence
Professional competence, seniority, and investment results
Obeying the law, confidentiality, and avoiding conflicts
quiz.explanation: All three bear directly on whether other people's money should be entrusted to this person.

quiz.question: Is a court conviction required for a Standard I(D) violation?
options: Yes, or at least a formal decision to prosecute by investigators
Yes, a judgment in force is needed before anything can be done
No, the conduct is enough without any criminal conviction
No, but a formal complaint from the injured party is required
quiz.explanation: The professional standard and the criminal standard differ - conduct can fall short of an offence and still show dishonesty.

quiz.question: Does an ordinary civil dispute fall under Standard I(D)?
options: No, because Standard I(D) applies only to criminal conduct
Yes, because every legal dispute affects professional standing
Yes, if the amount in dispute exceeds a certain threshold
No, unless it says something about honesty or competence
quiz.explanation: The standard does not judge the existence of a dispute; it examines whether conduct within it shows dishonesty.

quiz.question: Why does cheating in a university exam fall in scope?
options: Because it shows how someone behaves given an opportunity unobserved
Because all cheating is treated identically by the law
Because academic results form part of a professional record
Because CFA Institute requires the academic history declared
quiz.explanation: This is the logic of the whole standard: behaviour in one context predicts behaviour in another where the structure of temptation is the same.

quiz.question: When does substance misuse fall in scope?
options: In every case, since it is conduct falling below standards
When it affects the capacity to perform professional duties
Only when an authority has imposed a penalty
Never, since it is entirely a matter of private life
quiz.explanation: The standard does not judge a lifestyle - it asks whether the conduct leaves you unable to perform your duties.

keyTakeaways: Three criteria: honesty, trustworthiness, professional competence
Not a general code of personal morality
No criminal conviction is needed for a violation
The logic: behaviour in one context predicts behaviour in another
The final question is always: should other people's money go to this person

practicePrompt.question: A colleague is found to have falsified qualifications on a job application ten years ago. The matter has nothing to do with their current work. Does Standard I(D) apply?
options: No, it was too long ago and does not affect their current work
Yes: falsified qualifications belong to the honesty group, and the standard sets no limitation period
Only if the current firm suffered harm as a result
No, this is a matter between that person and their former employer
practicePrompt.explanation: Both negative options rest on criteria the standard does not use: how much time has passed, and whether harm resulted. The real criterion is the nature of the conduct - falsified qualifications sit squarely in the honesty group. That it happened at a different employer changes nothing either, because Standard I(D) is not limited to the current employment relationship.
